name: Bahrain
summary: The Central Bank of Bahrain (CBB) licenses and supervises banks and issues the CBB Rulebook; Volume 1 covers conventional banks (Volume 2, Islamic banks, is outside this map). AML/CFT rests on Decree-Law No. 4 of 2001, with suspicious transactions reported to the Ministry of Interior's financial intelligence unit, and personal data is governed by Law No. 30 of 2018 under the Personal Data Protection Authority. Explicit training duties verified in CBB texts cover director induction and ongoing training, senior management and compliance staff, compliance awareness sessions and cyber security training for all staff. The AML staff training chapter (Module FC-6) sits on the Rulebook host, which blocks automated access, so it is shown at competence pending a check.

regulators.name: Central Bank of Bahrain
regulators.role: Licenses, regulates and supervises banks and other financial institutions, issues the CBB Rulebook, supervises AML/CFT compliance and runs the Consumer Protection Office.

regulators.name: National Centre for Financial Intelligence (Ministry of Interior)
regulators.role: Bahrain's financial intelligence unit (formerly known as the Financial Intelligence Directorate) under the Ministry of Interior; receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports under Decree-Law 4 of 2001.

regulators.name: Personal Data Protection Authority
regulators.role: Supervises compliance with the Personal Data Protection Law (Law No. 30 of 2018), including by banks as data controllers.

regulators.name: National Cybersecurity Center (Ministry of Interior)
regulators.role: National cyber security authority; drafted the Financial Cybersecurity Controls standard that the CBB consulted on for all licensees.

programs.title: Bahrain | AML/CFT Staff Training under CBB Module FC and Decree-Law 4 of 2001
programs.why: Decree-Law 4 of 2001 obliges banks to keep identity and transaction records, report suspicions and follow the CBB's instructions on internal AML policies, procedures, controls and compliance officers. The CBB sets those instructions in Module FC, whose Chapter FC-6 covers staff training and recruitment (reported to require AML/CFT training for relevant new staff within three months and normally once a year after that). The FC-6 text sits on the CBB Rulebook host, which blocks automated access, so it could not be opened; the classification is held at competence until it is.

references.title: Decree-Law No. (4) of 2001 with respect to the Prevention and Prohibition of the Laundering of Money
references.note: Banks must keep client identity evidence and transaction records for five years, report suspicious transactions, and follow the regulator's instructions on internal AML policies, procedures, controls, management-level compliance officers and audit of those controls. The law itself sets no training duty.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Financial Crime Module (Module FC): copy issued with the 2023 consultation on amendments
references.note: CBB-hosted copy circulated with the 2023 FC amendments consultation. Its contents list shows Chapter FC-6 'Staff Training and Recruitment' (FC-6.1 last changed 01/2022), but FC-6 text is not reproduced in this copy.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1 (Conventional Banks)
references.provision: Module FC, Chapter FC-6 (Staff Training and Recruitment)
references.note: Module FC applies to all conventional bank licensees; FC-6.1 sets the staff training requirements. The in-force consolidated Rulebook is hosted at cbben.thomsonreuters.com, which refused automated access (403); the provision is cited from the Rulebook structure and not re-read here.

references.title: Risk Assessment: Guidance for Financial Institutions (October 2021)
references.note: Says institutions should resource and train relevant staff on AML/CFT/CPF measures in line with their risk assessment findings, and that training for onboarding, monitoring and screening staff is central to a strong compliance regime.

programs.title: Bahrain | Combating the Financing of Terrorism (Decree-Law 4/2001 and CBB TF Guidance)
programs.why: Terrorist financing is criminalised in Article 3 of Decree-Law 4 of 2001 as rewritten in 2017, and banks fall under the same reporting and control duties as for money laundering. The CBB's 2020 TF guidance expects relevant staff to be trained and kept current on TF risks and their responsibilities, which supports the Module FC training rules; guidance alone does not create a separate binding course requirement.

references.title: Decree-Law No. (36) of 2017 amending Article (3) of Decree-Law No. (4) of 2001
references.note: Replaced the terrorist financing offence in Article 3(1-3): collecting, providing or allocating funds for a terrorist group or individual terrorist is punishable by long imprisonment and heavy fines (CBB-hosted English copy of the Official Gazette text).

references.title: Combating the Financing of Terrorism: Guidance for Financial Institutions (November 2020)
references.note: Guidance to be read with Module FC; among the measures it lists, institutions should make TF detection part of the compliance programme and keep relevant staff trained and up to date on TF risks and their own responsibilities.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1 (Conventional Banks)
references.provision: Module FC, Chapters FC-6 and FC-8
references.note: FC-8 covers terrorist financing and designated persons; FC-6 covers staff training. The in-force consolidated Rulebook is hosted at cbben.thomsonreuters.com, which refused automated access (403); the provision is cited from the Rulebook structure and not re-read here.

programs.title: Bahrain | Countering Proliferation Financing (CBB PF Guidance)
programs.why: The CBB's PF guidance explains UN proliferation sanctions and red flags, and its 2021 risk assessment guidance says PF and sanctions-evasion awareness can be built into existing sanctions or AML/CFT training. No binding PF-specific training rule was verified.

references.title: Countering Proliferation Financing: Guidance for Financial Institutions (November 2019)
references.note: Explains UN Security Council PF sanctions, says all institutions must screen names and addresses against UN designation lists, and gives PF red-flag indicators; it sets no separate training rule.

references.title: Risk Assessment: Guidance for Financial Institutions (October 2021)
references.note: Asks institutions to assess proliferation financing risk alongside ML/TF and suggests that staff awareness of PF typologies and sanctions evasion be added to sanctions or AML/CFT training.

programs.title: Bahrain | Customer Due Diligence under CBB Module FC
programs.why: Module FC, Chapter FC-1, sets detailed customer due diligence rules for conventional banks, including what to do when due diligence cannot be completed and extra criteria for non-resident customers. Staff who open and maintain accounts need to know these rules; training itself sits in FC-6, which could not be opened.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Financial Crime Module (Module FC): copy issued with the 2023 consultation on amendments
references.note: If due diligence cannot be completed the bank must consider freezing funds and filing an STR, ending the relationship, not proceeding, or returning funds by the same method; retail banks must have documented acceptance criteria and approved policies for non-resident customers.

references.title: Decree-Law No. (4) of 2001 with respect to the Prevention and Prohibition of the Laundering of Money
references.note: Identity evidence for each client must be kept for five years after the relationship ends.

programs.title: Bahrain | Enhanced Due Diligence for Higher-Risk Customers (Module FC-1.3)
programs.why: Module FC requires enhanced due diligence for customers with a higher risk profile and lists the additional steps (source of funds and wealth, senior management approval, enhanced monitoring and more). Applying it consistently depends on staff knowing when and how to escalate.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Financial Crime Module (Module FC): copy issued with the 2023 consultation on amendments
references.note: Enhanced due diligence is mandatory for higher-risk customers; the guidance lists measures such as more information on the customer and purpose, source of funds and wealth, senior management approval and closer monitoring.

programs.title: Bahrain | Beneficial Ownership Identification (CBB BO Guidance)
programs.why: Identifying the beneficial owners of companies and trusts is part of the Module FC due diligence rules, and the CBB has issued guidance on how to do it. No separate training rule applies, but staff handling legal-person customers need the knowledge.

references.title: Beneficial Ownership: Guidance for Financial Institutions (November 2021)
references.note: Guidance on identifying and verifying the beneficial owners of legal persons and arrangements such as trusts, drawn from FATF material and to be read with CBB rules.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Financial Crime Module (Module FC): copy issued with the 2023 consultation on amendments
references.note: Customer due diligence rules covering identity of customers and their beneficial owners, including companies under formation (2023 amendments).

programs.title: Bahrain | Targeted Financial Sanctions and UN List Screening
programs.why: CBB guidance says all institutions must screen against UN designation lists and suggests sanctions-evasion and PF-TFS awareness be included in sanctions training. The binding designated-persons rules are in Module FC, Chapter FC-8, which could not be opened, so no express training duty is recorded.

references.title: Countering Proliferation Financing: Guidance for Financial Institutions (November 2019)
references.note: Explains UN Security Council PF sanctions, says all institutions must screen names and addresses against UN designation lists, and gives PF red-flag indicators; it sets no separate training rule.

references.title: Risk Assessment: Guidance for Financial Institutions (October 2021)
references.note: Covers sanctions-evasion risk and recommends that training on targeted financial sanctions typologies be rolled into sanctions or AML/CFT modules.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1 (Conventional Banks)
references.provision: Module FC, Section FC-8.3 (Designated Persons and Entities)
references.note: The in-force consolidated Rulebook is hosted at cbben.thomsonreuters.com, which refused automated access (403); the provision is cited from the Rulebook structure and not re-read here.

programs.title: Bahrain | Suspicious Transaction Reporting (Decree-Law 4/2001, Module FC-5)
programs.why: The AML law requires banks to report suspected transactions to the enforcement unit and the relevant authorities, and Module FC-5 sets internal and external reporting procedures. Staff must recognise and escalate suspicion; the training rule itself is in FC-6, which could not be opened.

references.title: Decree-Law No. (4) of 2001 with respect to the Prevention and Prohibition of the Laundering of Money
references.note: Banks must report suspected transactions to the Enforcement Unit and relevant authorities and give the Unit further information or help on request.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Financial Crime Module (Module FC): copy issued with the 2023 consultation on amendments
references.note: Lists internal reporting (FC-5.1), external reporting (FC-5.2) and contacting the authorities (FC-5.3) and an STR form in the appendices.

programs.title: Bahrain | Trade-Based Money Laundering Awareness (CBB TBML Guidance)
programs.why: The CBB's 2023 TBML guidance sets out trends, red flags and best practices for banks financing trade. It is guidance; no specific training duty was verified.

references.title: Trade-Based Money Laundering: Guidance for Financial Institutions (February 2023)
references.note: Describes the trade finance environment, TBML trends, risk indicators and best practices for banks handling trade transactions.

programs.title: Bahrain | AML/CFT/CPF Risk-Based Approach and Risk Assessment
programs.why: CBB risk assessment guidance explains how institutions should identify, assess, evaluate and mitigate ML, TF and PF risks and train staff on the resulting measures. The binding risk assessment rule in Module FC was not opened, so this is recorded as good practice.

references.title: Risk Assessment: Guidance for Financial Institutions (October 2021)
references.note: Sets out the steps of an institutional ML/TF/PF risk assessment and says staff should be trained on the AML/CFT/CPF measures that follow from it.

programs.title: Bahrain | AML Record-Keeping (Decree-Law 4/2001 Article 5, Module FC-7)
programs.why: The AML law fixes a five-year retention period for identity evidence and transaction records, and Module FC-7 adds the CBB's record-keeping rules. Staff who create and keep records must know the periods and formats; no separate training duty was found.

references.title: Decree-Law No. (4) of 2001 with respect to the Prevention and Prohibition of the Laundering of Money
references.note: Identity evidence must be kept for five years after the relationship ends and transaction records for five years after the transaction ends.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Financial Crime Module (Module FC): copy issued with the 2023 consultation on amendments
references.note: Shows FC-7 Record-Keeping (general requirements, last changed 01/2019).

programs.title: Bahrain | AML/CFT for Frontline and Branch Staff
programs.why: Frontline staff carry out customer identification and spot unusual activity. Module FC-6 is reported to require AML/CFT training for relevant staff on joining and normally each year, but the Rulebook text could not be opened, so this stays at competence.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1 (Conventional Banks)
references.note: The in-force consolidated Rulebook is hosted at cbben.thomsonreuters.com, which refused automated access (403); the provision is cited from the Rulebook structure and not re-read here.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Financial Crime Module (Module FC): copy issued with the 2023 consultation on amendments
references.note: CBB-hosted copy circulated with the 2023 FC amendments consultation. Its contents list shows Chapter FC-6 'Staff Training and Recruitment' (FC-6.1 last changed 01/2022), but FC-6 text is not reproduced in this copy.

programs.title: Bahrain | AML/CFT Oversight for Board and Senior Management
programs.why: The AML law requires management-level compliance officers and internal controls, and the revised HC module asks boards to approve policies and promote risk awareness. Board-level AML training is not separately prescribed in the texts opened; general director training is covered under program 35.

references.title: Decree-Law No. (4) of 2001 with respect to the Prevention and Prohibition of the Laundering of Money
references.note: Banks must follow regulator instructions on internal AML policies and controls, including management-level compliance officers and audit of those controls.

references.title: High-Level Controls Module (Module HC) for bank licensees: revised module issued for consultation, July 2022
references.note: The board must promote risk awareness within a strong risk culture and make clear that all staff must operate within the approved risk appetite.

programs.title: Bahrain | Fraud Awareness: Customer Communication and Link Security (Module OM-5.5)
programs.why: Module OM requires banks to limit clickable links in customer messages, use one private email domain and run customer awareness campaigns on link-based fraud. These are control and customer-education duties, not a staff training rule.

references.title: Operational Risk Management Module (Module OM), Volume 1: copy issued with the January 2024 consultation on cyber security amendments
references.note: Banks must use a single private email domain, restrict links in SMS and similar messages to customer-initiated cases, avoid shortened links and run customer awareness campaigns on fraud via links.

programs.title: Bahrain | Compliance Awareness Sessions led by the Compliance Officer (Module HC-8)
programs.why: The revised HC module makes the compliance officer responsible for written guidance to staff on applying laws and regulations and for awareness sessions for staff on compliance policy, run under the CEO's sponsorship. The provision is taken from the CBB-hosted consultation text of the module, which the Rulebook shows in force for conventional banks since April 2023.

references.title: High-Level Controls Module (Module HC) for bank licensees: revised module issued for consultation, July 2022
references.note: The compliance officer must give staff written guidance on applying laws and regulations and, sponsored by the CEO, run awareness sessions for staff on compliance policy requirements and issues. CBB-hosted consultation text; the in-force Rulebook text was not opened.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1 (Conventional Banks)
references.note: The in-force consolidated Rulebook is hosted at cbben.thomsonreuters.com, which refused automated access (403); the provision is cited from the Rulebook structure and not re-read here.

programs.title: Bahrain | Corporate Governance under the High-Level Controls Module
programs.why: The revised HC module sets the board's overall responsibilities, board formation, committees, risk, compliance and audit functions for all bank licensees. It expects directors and managers to understand their governance roles; specific training duties are mapped under programs 35 and 36.

references.title: High-Level Controls Module (Module HC) for bank licensees: revised module issued for consultation, July 2022
references.note: Sets the board's responsibilities and says board members must understand their oversight and governance role and be able to judge the bank's affairs objectively.

programs.title: Bahrain | Board Director Induction and Ongoing Training (Modules HC and FP)
programs.why: The HC module requires the board to fund induction programmes every year and to make sure each new director gets a formal, tailored induction and access to ongoing training, and directors must keep educating themselves on the business and governance. Module FP (in force 2025) adds that licensees must arrange induction and continuing professional development for directors.

references.title: High-Level Controls Module (Module HC) for bank licensees: revised module issued for consultation, July 2022
references.note: Board must allocate time and budget each year for director induction, give every new director a tailored induction with access to ongoing training, and invite continuing directors to orientation; all directors must keep educating themselves. CBB-hosted consultation text, shown in force since April 2023.

references.title: Fit and Proper Requirements Module (Module FP), Common Volume: consultation version, October 2024
references.note: Licensees must set up induction and ongoing training and CPD for board directors on the business, the industry and compliance duties. Paragraph numbers are from the consultation version.

references.title: CBB introduces new fit and proper requirements for board and management of licensed financial institutions (press release, 4 March 2025)
references.note: Confirms that Module FP was issued in the Common Volume for all licensees, replacing the fit and proper parts of the LR, AU and TC modules; prior-approval rules apply from 1 April 2025 and the remaining rules from 1 October 2025. Boards and CEOs answer for the suitability of senior managers under licensee-set standards.

programs.title: Bahrain | Senior Management Competence and Annual Training Plans (Modules HC and FP)
programs.why: The HC module says senior managers must receive regular training to keep their competence current. Module FP adds an annual assessment of training needs for heads of senior management functions, an annual training plan and at least 15 hours of CPD a year (consultation text; the final module took effect in 2025).

references.title: High-Level Controls Module (Module HC) for bank licensees: revised module issued for consultation, July 2022
references.note: Senior managers must have the experience, competence and integrity for their roles and receive regular training to stay current in their areas.

references.title: Fit and Proper Requirements Module (Module FP), Common Volume: consultation version, October 2024
references.note: Licensees must assess yearly the training needs of heads of senior management functions and keep an annual plan covering needs, methods, deadlines, review and at least 15 CPD hours a year. Consultation version; the final paragraph may differ.

references.title: CBB introduces new fit and proper requirements for board and management of licensed financial institutions (press release, 4 March 2025)
references.note: Confirms that Module FP was issued in the Common Volume for all licensees, replacing the fit and proper parts of the LR, AU and TC modules; prior-approval rules apply from 1 April 2025 and the remaining rules from 1 October 2025. Boards and CEOs answer for the suitability of senior managers under licensee-set standards.

programs.title: Bahrain | Fit and Proper Requirements (Module FP and CBB Law Article 65)
programs.why: The CBB Law requires prior CBB approval of board nominees and executives and lets the CBB set qualification, experience and training standards. Module FP, issued in March 2025, puts fit and proper rules for all licensees in one place and requires board-approved recruitment, training and competency policies with periodic competency assessments.

references.title: Central Bank of Bahrain and Financial Institutions Law (Law No. 64 of 2006)
references.note: Board nominees and executive posts need prior CBB approval; the CBB may set qualification, experience and training standards for officers and staff and can require removal of unsuitable officials.

references.title: Fit and Proper Requirements Module (Module FP), Common Volume: consultation version, October 2024
references.note: Licensees must keep unsuitable people out of board and senior roles, assess candidates before appointment, re-check ongoing suitability and adopt board-approved recruitment, training and competency policies with periodic competency assessments.

references.title: CBB introduces new fit and proper requirements for board and management of licensed financial institutions (press release, 4 March 2025)
references.note: Confirms that Module FP was issued in the Common Volume for all licensees, replacing the fit and proper parts of the LR, AU and TC modules; prior-approval rules apply from 1 April 2025 and the remaining rules from 1 October 2025. Boards and CEOs answer for the suitability of senior managers under licensee-set standards.

programs.title: Bahrain | Code of Conduct and Corporate Values (Module HC-1.2)
programs.why: The board must approve a code of conduct for directors, managers and staff, make sure the values and code are communicated throughout the bank and that everyone knows misconduct leads to disciplinary action. This is a communication duty rather than a prescribed course.

references.title: High-Level Controls Module (Module HC) for bank licensees: revised module issued for consultation, July 2022
references.note: The board approves a code of conduct, sets ethical values, promotes risk awareness, ensures the code is communicated across the bank and that staff know breaches lead to discipline.

programs.title: Bahrain | Whistleblowing Policy and Protection (Module HC-1.2)
programs.why: Banks must have a board-approved, well-communicated whistleblowing policy that lets staff raise concerns confidentially without reprisal, including escalation to the CBB, and the board must protect those who speak up. Staff need to know the channel; no separate training is prescribed.

references.title: High-Level Controls Module (Module HC) for bank licensees: revised module issued for consultation, July 2022
references.note: Staff must be able to raise concerns confidentially and without reprisal through a well-communicated whistleblowing policy; the board oversees it, protects whistleblowers and decides how concerns are investigated.

programs.title: Bahrain | Compliance Function Staff Training (Module HC-8.1.9)
programs.why: The revised HC module requires compliance staff to have the right qualifications and a sound understanding of applicable law, and to receive regular and systematic training to stay up to date with legal and regulatory developments.

references.title: High-Level Controls Module (Module HC) for bank licensees: revised module issued for consultation, July 2022
references.note: Compliance staff must be qualified, understand the laws and standards that apply to the bank and receive regular, systematic training on developments.

programs.title: Bahrain | Internal Audit and Risk Function Staff Training (Module HC)
programs.why: The head of internal audit must arrange ongoing training for audit staff as products and processes grow more complex, and the risk management function must have enough qualified staff who receive regular training.

references.title: High-Level Controls Module (Module HC) for bank licensees: revised module issued for consultation, July 2022
references.note: The head of internal audit must arrange ongoing training for audit staff; the risk management function must be staffed with qualified people who receive regular training.

programs.title: Bahrain | CBB Consumer Protection and Business Conduct (Module BC)
programs.why: Module BC sets conduct rules for conventional banks, including non-discriminatory service, promotions and advertising, disclosure of charges, complaints and services for disabled customers, and the CBB runs a Consumer Protection Office for escalated complaints. Staff must apply these rules; no general consumer-protection training duty was confirmed in the texts opened.

references.title: Business and Market Conduct Module (Module BC), Volume 1: copy issued with the November 2023 second consultation
references.note: Its contents list confirms the conduct chapters for conventional banks, including non-discriminatory service (BC-B), client confidentiality (BC-3), customer complaints procedures (BC-9) and services for disabled customers (BC-10); the copy reproduces only the amended section on insurance cover on loans.

references.title: CBB Official Complaints Procedures: Banks / Financial Institutions / Capital Markets
references.note: Customers first complain to the bank, which must acknowledge within 5 business days and answer in writing within 4 weeks; an unsatisfied customer can then escalate to the CBB Consumer Protection Office with the bank's reply.

programs.title: Bahrain | Customer Complaints Handling (Module BC-9)
programs.why: Banks must handle complaints under documented procedures and meet CBB timelines (acknowledgement within 5 business days, written answer within 4 weeks). BC-9.4.2 is reported to require that relevant staff know the internal complaint procedures and are trained periodically, but the Rulebook text could not be opened, so this stays at competence.

references.title: CBB Official Complaints Procedures: Banks / Financial Institutions / Capital Markets
references.note: Customers first complain to the bank, which must acknowledge within 5 business days and answer in writing within 4 weeks; an unsatisfied customer can then escalate to the CBB Consumer Protection Office with the bank's reply.

references.title: Business and Market Conduct Module (Module BC), Volume 1: copy issued with the November 2023 second consultation
references.note: Its contents list confirms the conduct chapters for conventional banks, including non-discriminatory service (BC-B), client confidentiality (BC-3), customer complaints procedures (BC-9) and services for disabled customers (BC-10); the copy reproduces only the amended section on insurance cover on loans.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1 (Conventional Banks)
references.note: The in-force consolidated Rulebook is hosted at cbben.thomsonreuters.com, which refused automated access (403); the provision is cited from the Rulebook structure and not re-read here.

programs.title: Bahrain | Serving Customers with Disabilities (Module BC-10)
programs.why: Chapter BC-10 sets measures for Bahraini retail banks serving disabled customers, including visually and hearing impaired customers, and is reported to require specialised training for staff who deal with them as part of their overall training. The Rulebook text could not be opened, so it is held at competence.

references.title: Business and Market Conduct Module (Module BC), Volume 1: copy issued with the November 2023 second consultation
references.note: Its contents list confirms the conduct chapters for conventional banks, including non-discriminatory service (BC-B), client confidentiality (BC-3), customer complaints procedures (BC-9) and services for disabled customers (BC-10); the copy reproduces only the amended section on insurance cover on loans.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1 (Conventional Banks)
references.note: The in-force consolidated Rulebook is hosted at cbben.thomsonreuters.com, which refused automated access (403); the provision is cited from the Rulebook structure and not re-read here.

programs.title: Bahrain | Customer Confidentiality (CBB Law Articles 116-117)
programs.why: The CBB Law forbids licensees from disclosing information on customers' private affairs except with the customer's clear consent, under law or treaty, by court order or on CBB instruction. Every employee handling customer data must understand these limits; no training duty is attached.

references.title: Central Bank of Bahrain and Financial Institutions Law (Law No. 64 of 2006)
references.note: Customer information is confidential and may only be disclosed with the customer's clear consent, under a law or treaty, under a court order or to carry out a CBB instruction.

references.title: Business and Market Conduct Module (Module BC), Volume 1: copy issued with the November 2023 second consultation
references.note: Its contents list confirms the conduct chapters for conventional banks, including non-discriminatory service (BC-B), client confidentiality (BC-3), customer complaints procedures (BC-9) and services for disabled customers (BC-10); the copy reproduces only the amended section on insurance cover on loans.

programs.title: Bahrain | Organisation-wide Information Security Awareness (Module OM-5.5)
programs.why: Module OM makes an organisation-wide security awareness programme a required part of the cyber security risk management framework, and boards receive regular reports on the status of staff information security awareness. Text read from the CBB-hosted copy of Module OM issued with the January 2024 consultation.

references.title: Operational Risk Management Module (Module OM), Volume 1: copy issued with the January 2024 consultation on cyber security amendments
references.note: The board must ensure the cyber framework includes a strategy, a policy, a risk approach and an organisation-wide security awareness programme; board reports should cover staff awareness status.

programs.title: Bahrain | Cyber Security Training for All Employees (Module OM-5.5)
programs.why: Banks must give all employees adequate, regular cyber security training on the threats they may meet (for example by testing reactions to simulated attacks), keep staff informed of current breaches and threats, give extra training to higher-risk staff and check that awareness actually improves.

references.title: Operational Risk Management Module (Module OM), Volume 1: copy issued with the January 2024 consultation on cyber security amendments
references.note: Banks must measure improvement in staff cyber awareness and give all employees regular cyber training, including simulated attack testing, with extra training for higher-risk staff.

references.title: Financial Cybersecurity Controls (National Cybersecurity Center draft v0.1, issued by the CBB for consultation)
references.issuer: Ministry of Interior, National Cybersecurity Center / Central Bank of Bahrain
references.note: Draft national standard that the CBB said would be built into all Rulebook volumes. Subdomain 1.7 would require an approved awareness programme for staff, third parties and customers, role-based training (partly at orientation) and an annual review of the programme's effectiveness. Status as a final standard not confirmed.

programs.title: Bahrain | Cyber Security Risk Management for Cyber and IT Staff (Module OM-5.5)
programs.why: Senior management must ensure cyber security staff attend regular update and training sessions, and banks must provide regular role-specific cyber training for cyber security roles, IT staff and other high-risk staff.

references.title: Operational Risk Management Module (Module OM), Volume 1: copy issued with the January 2024 consultation on cyber security amendments
references.note: Cyber security staff must attend regular update and certification-level training; role-specific cyber training must be given regularly to executive management, cyber roles, IT staff and high-risk staff.

programs.title: Bahrain | Personal Data Protection Law (Law No. 30 of 2018)
programs.why: Bahrain's PDPL governs the processing of personal data and is supervised by the Personal Data Protection Authority. Banks must apply its principles and security duties, which requires staff knowledge, but the official text could not be opened from this session, so no training duty is claimed.

references.title: Law No. (30) of 2018 with respect to Personal Data Protection
references.issuer: Kingdom of Bahrain (Legislation and Legal Opinion Commission)
references.note: General data protection law for processing of personal data, supervised by the Personal Data Protection Authority. The Commission's English text could not be opened from this session (host not reachable), so no training duty has been confirmed.

programs.title: Bahrain | Phishing and Social Engineering Resilience (Module OM-5.5)
programs.why: Regular cyber training under OM-5.5.55 may include testing staff reactions to simulated attacks, and OM-5.5.21 sets anti-phishing controls for customer emails and messages. Phishing training is not named as a separate requirement, so it is recorded as part of the wider cyber training duty.

references.title: Operational Risk Management Module (Module OM), Volume 1: copy issued with the January 2024 consultation on cyber security amendments
references.note: Anti-phishing controls for customer messages (private email domain, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, restricted links) and regular staff cyber training that can include simulated attacks.

references.title: Financial Cybersecurity Controls (National Cybersecurity Center draft v0.1, issued by the CBB for consultation)
references.issuer: Ministry of Interior, National Cybersecurity Center / Central Bank of Bahrain
references.note: Draft national standard that the CBB said would be built into all Rulebook volumes. Subdomain 1.7 would require an approved awareness programme for staff, third parties and customers, role-based training (partly at orientation) and an annual review of the programme's effectiveness. Status as a final standard not confirmed.

programs.title: Bahrain | Cyber Incident Response and Reporting to the CBB (Module OM-5.5)
programs.why: Banks must run incident response exercises (simulations, war games, table-tops) with technical staff, crisis teams and decision-makers, contact the CBB within one hour of a qualifying cyber incident and file the incident report in two stages. These duties require trained responders but no separate course is prescribed.

references.title: Operational Risk Management Module (Module OM), Volume 1: copy issued with the January 2024 consultation on cyber security amendments
references.note: Banks must exercise response plans with relevant staff, call the CBB within one hour of a cyber incident affecting customer data or critical services, send Section A of the report within two hours and Section B within 10 calendar days.

programs.title: Bahrain | ICT and Cyber Risk Management Framework (Module OM-5.5)
programs.why: Banks must run a cyber security risk management framework based on the NIST framework, approved by the board and reviewed at least every three years, with senior management keeping asset inventories and adequate cyber staffing. The framework requires competent staff but sets no separate training beyond programs 72 and 73.

references.title: Operational Risk Management Module (Module OM), Volume 1: copy issued with the January 2024 consultation on cyber security amendments
references.note: Framework components, NIST alignment, board approval at least every three years and senior management duties on asset ownership, inventories and cyber staffing.

programs.title: Bahrain | Cyber Security Training for the Board and Senior Management (Module OM-5.5.56)
programs.why: Role-specific cyber security training must be provided regularly to the executive board and senior management, and boards must discuss cyber security and receive regular cyber reports.

references.title: Operational Risk Management Module (Module OM), Volume 1: copy issued with the January 2024 consultation on cyber security amendments
references.note: Cyber security must be a board agenda item, boards receive regular cyber reports, and the executive board and senior management must receive regular role-specific cyber training.

programs.title: Bahrain | Enterprise Risk Management and the Risk Function (Module HC-7)
programs.why: Module HC makes Bahraini banks run an independent risk management function, led by a CRO, that implements an enterprise-wide risk governance framework, and requires that function to be staffed with qualified people who receive regular training. Risk staff and the committee they report to need a shared understanding of the bank's framework, limits and escalation routes.

references.title: CBB Rulebook (Bank Licensees), High-Level Controls Module HC, consultation text of 18 July 2022
references.note: The risk function must have enough experienced and qualified staff who are subject to regular training, and must implement an enterprise-wide risk governance framework with policies, procedures and limits. Read from the July 2022 consultation copy; the revised module applied from 1 October 2023.

programs.title: Bahrain | Credit Risk Management under Module CM
programs.why: The revised Credit Risk Management Module (issued May 2021, in force from 1 July 2022 and amended since) makes senior management responsible for confirming that everyone involved in a credit relationship has the knowledge, skills and experience to keep it within policy. No separate course is prescribed, so this is a competence duty.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module CM (Credit Risk Management), revised module consultation draft dated January 2019
references.note: Senior management must be satisfied that staff handling any credit relationship have the knowledge, skills and experience to meet the bank's policies. Final numbering differs: the in-force text puts the framework in CM-1.2 (last changed 10/2022).

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module CM, Exposure Limit Rules consultation draft (XX 2025) with current table of contents
references.note: Shows the current structure of Module CM: framework, granting, measurement and monitoring, administration and collateral, NPL management, reporting and classification and provisioning.

references.title: CBB Annual Report 2021
references.note: Records that the revised Module CM was issued in May 2021 and became effective on 1 July 2022, replacing the earlier module.

programs.title: Bahrain | Liquidity Risk Management, LCR and NSFR (Module LM)
programs.why: Module LM requires the board to make sure that senior management and the staff who measure, monitor and control liquidity risk are competent, and that independent, skilled staff run the controls; it also sets the LCR, NSFR and loans-to-deposit rules treasury staff must apply. In April 2026 the CBB temporarily eased the LCR and NSFR minimums as part of a support package.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module LM (Liquidity Risk Management), consultation text dated December 2017
references.note: Board must ensure competence of senior management and liquidity risk personnel, and that internal controls are run by independent staff with the necessary skills; ALCO should be supported by competent risk managers. The module was finalised in August 2018.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module LM, March 2021 consultation copy (Loans to Deposit Ratio section) with contents list
references.note: Contents show LM-1 governance last changed 08/2018, LCR in LM-11, NSFR in LM-12 and a proposed loans-to-deposit ratio in LM-13.

references.title: CBB announces Loan Deferral Program with BHD 7 billion liquidity support (13 April 2026)
references.note: Announces lower minimum LCR and NSFR (from 100% to 80%) and a lower reserve requirement as temporary relief measures.

programs.title: Bahrain | Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book (proposed Module IR)
programs.why: The CBB consulted in January 2024 on a new IRRBB module for conventional banks requiring board and senior management oversight, limits, stress scenarios and documented modelling assumptions that the board understands. The CBB's 2024 annual report says feedback was still under study, so the text is a draft; it signals the competence banks are expected to build.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, proposed Module IR (Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book), consultation draft dated xx/2024
references.note: Draft rules: board and senior management oversight of IRRBB, limits and escalation, internal shock scenarios, and key assumptions documented and clearly understood by the board.

references.title: Circular OG/17/2024: Consultation on Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book Module
references.note: Consultation sent to all conventional banks on 16 January 2024, comments due 31 March 2024.

references.title: CBB Annual Report 2024
references.note: Reports that industry feedback on the IR module was received and remained under study.

programs.title: Bahrain | Capital Adequacy and Basel III (Module CA)
programs.why: Module CA sets the Basel III capital rules for conventional banks, and the CBB has been revising the credit risk part (consultations in August 2023 and July 2024) and initial capital levels (February 2026). Staff who compute risk weights and capital ratios must keep up with these drafts; no training duty is stated.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module CA Part 2 (Credit Risk), second consultation draft of 8 July 2024
references.note: Proposed revised standardised approach to credit risk, building on the August 2023 draft.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module LR, consultation extract on initial capital (February 2026)
references.note: Proposed revision of the financial resources and capital adequacy licensing condition for conventional banks.

references.title: CBB Annual Report 2024
references.note: Second CA consultation (July 2024) feedback was under review at the time of the report.

programs.title: Bahrain | Stress Testing Programme (Module ST)
programs.why: Module ST took effect in July 2018 and requires banks to run a stress testing programme, report results to the CBB twice a year and have the framework independently reviewed. When banks asked the CBB for training, it replied that each bank must arrange its own competency building according to its training needs, so competence rests with the bank.

references.title: Circular EDBS/KH/44/2018: Risk Management Related Modules (DS, RR, ICAAP and ST)
references.note: Lists Module ST as effective July 2018, with stress test results due to the CBB on 31 May and 30 November each year from 2019 and an independent review of the framework.

references.title: Feedback statement: Consultation for Proposed Stress Testing Module (ST), June 2018
references.note: In answer to a request for CBB training, the CBB said each bank must arrange competency enhancements based on its own training needs.

programs.title: Bahrain | Risk Appetite Framework (Module HC)
audience: Chief risk officer and risk staff
programs.why: Module HC makes the board, with senior management and the CRO, set the bank's risk appetite and oversee adherence to it, and requires the risk function to monitor exposures against that appetite with early warnings for breaches. Those involved need to understand how the appetite is expressed and escalated; no course is prescribed.

references.title: CBB Rulebook (Bank Licensees), High-Level Controls Module HC, consultation text of 18 July 2022
references.note: The board sets the risk appetite with management and the CRO and oversees adherence; the risk function monitors against the appetite and runs an early-warning system for breaches.

programs.title: Bahrain | Large Exposures and Credit Concentration (Module CM-2)
programs.why: Chapter CM-2 limits large and related-party exposures and requires a board-approved policy on concentration; in March 2025 the CBB consulted on replacing it with new exposure limit rules aligned with Basel. Credit and reporting staff need to know how exposures and connected counterparties are measured.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module CM, Exposure Limit Rules consultation draft (XX 2025) with current table of contents
references.note: Proposed rules on measuring exposures, large exposure limits, related parties, exempt exposures, reporting and credit concentration, and on exposures to board members and employees.

references.title: Circular OG/91/2025: Consultation on Proposed Amendments to the Credit Risk Management Module
references.note: Issued 18 March 2025 to all Bahraini bank licensees; the new exposure limit rules would replace the large exposure and connected counterparty requirements in CM-2. Comments were due 17 April 2025.

programs.title: Bahrain | Reputational Risk Management (Module RR)
programs.why: Module RR, issued in July 2018, requires each bank's reputational risk governance framework to include raising employees' risk awareness and giving them adequate training, alongside codes of conduct and controls. The final text sits on the blocked Rulebook host; the duty is read from the CBB-hosted consultation text, which the CBB's feedback statement kept. The training wording comes from the 2018 consultation copy; the in-force Module RR text is on the blocked Rulebook host, so this stays at competence until it is checked.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module RR (Reputational Risk Management), consultation text of 24 April 2018
references.note: The bank's governance framework must include raising employees' risk awareness and providing them with adequate training.

references.title: Feedback statement: Reputational Risk Management Module, June 2018
references.note: Shows RR-3.1.8, including the training element, retained after consultation.

references.title: Circular EDBS/KH/44/2018: Risk Management Related Modules (DS, RR, ICAAP and ST)
references.note: Confirms Module RR was issued as part of Rulebook Volumes 1 and 2 with effect from July 2018.

programs.title: Bahrain | Outsourcing and Cloud Outsourcing Requirements (Module OM-2)
programs.why: The CBB's July 2022 outsourcing rules bar outsourcing of compliance, AML/CFT, financial control and risk management, set approval and notification steps and require an approved person to coordinate and monitor each arrangement. A 2021 draft chapter on cloud outsourcing would have required key staff to be kept up to date by training, but that chapter does not appear in the 2024 contents of Module OM, so it is not treated as in force.

references.title: CBB Outsourcing Requirements, consultation text (April 2022)
references.note: Lists functions that cannot be outsourced, prior approval and notification rules, SLA content, and the designation of an approved person as coordinator for each arrangement.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module OM, January 2024 consultation copy with contents list
references.note: Contents show OM-2.1 Outsourcing Arrangements last changed 04/2023 and the former OM-2.2 to OM-2.8 deleted in July 2022.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, proposed Chapter OM-2A Cloud Outsourcing Arrangements, consultation draft (July 2021)
references.note: Draft required banks to name key staff for cloud arrangements and keep their knowledge current through training or other means; adoption not confirmed.

references.title: CBB Annual Report 2022
references.note: Records issue of the revised outsourcing requirements in July 2022.

programs.title: Bahrain | Business Continuity and Cyber Resilience (Module OM-4 and OM-5.5)
programs.why: Module OM-4 sets business continuity management rules, including testing and review, and OM-5.5.52 requires the continuity plan to include recovery from cyber incidents. Staff must know their roles in the plan, but no separate training rule was confirmed in the text opened.

references.title: Operational Risk Management Module (Module OM), Volume 1: copy issued with the January 2024 consultation on cyber security amendments
references.provision: Chapter OM-4 (table of contents) and OM-5.5.52
references.note: Lists the BCM chapter (plan development, recovery objectives, testing and review) and requires the BCP to include recovery of systems and services after a cyber incident.

programs.title: Bahrain | Recovery and Resolution Planning (Module DS)
programs.why: Module DS (July 2018) sets recovery plan rules for all Bahraini banks and fuller recovery and resolution planning for domestic systemically important banks, whose plans the CBB reviews each year. Staff who prepare or would execute the plan need to know its triggers and options; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Circular EDBS/KH/44/2018: Risk Management Related Modules (DS, RR, ICAAP and ST)
references.note: Module DS covers D-SIB obligations and recovery plans; recovery plan requirements apply to all Bahraini bank licensees, and D-SIBs submit recovery and resolution plans to a CBB due date.

references.title: CBB Annual Report 2021
references.provision: Chapter 2, Amendments related to the submission of Recovery and Resolution Plans
references.note: May 2021 amendments to Modules DS and ICAAP set due dates for submitting recovery and resolution plans.

references.title: CBB Annual Report 2024
references.note: The CBB reviewed D-SIBs' recovery and resolution plans, which are submitted annually.

programs.title: Bahrain | Credit Appraisal and Credit Officer Competence (Module CM)
programs.why: Module CM expects each credit proposal to be analysed by an experienced analyst, credit officers to have the experience and knowledge to judge credit risk, and a board-approved policy on the information needed to approve or renew credit. These are competence requirements for credit roles, not a set course.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module CM (Credit Risk Management), revised module consultation draft dated January 2019
references.note: Credit proposals must be analysed by an experienced analyst; credit risk officers must have the experience, knowledge and background for prudent judgment; the credit committee should be made up of senior, experienced officers.

programs.title: Bahrain | Non-Performing Loans Strategy and Workout (Module CM)
programs.why: Banks must have an NPL strategy and policy, assess their internal capability to reduce NPLs, and give responsibility for problem credits to a specialised workout unit. In February 2023 the CBB amended the NPL rules (purchased or originated credit-impaired exposures, re-staging of retail exposures).

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module CM (Credit Risk Management), revised module consultation draft dated January 2019
references.note: Defines non-performing exposures (all treated as Stage 3), exit criteria, and requires an NPL strategy, a workout section and an assessment of internal capabilities. In-force NPL rules are in CM-1.6 (07/2021).

references.title: CBB Annual Report 2023
references.provision: Chapter 2, Amendments to the Credit Risk Management Module
references.note: February 2023 amendments added POCI exposures to non-performing exposures and allowed re-staging of certain retail exposures from Stage 3 to Stage 2.

programs.title: Bahrain | Classification, ECL Provisioning and IFRS 9 (Module CM-1.8)
programs.why: The board and senior management must ensure sound ECL methodologies under IFRS 9, a board-approved provisioning policy sent to the CBB, and documented use of experienced credit judgment. Since January 2023 sovereign exposures also use IFRS 9 ECL. Staff applying staging and overlays need this knowledge; no course is prescribed.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module CM (Credit Risk Management), revised module consultation draft dated January 2019
references.note: Board and senior management responsibility for adequate allowances, a board-approved ECL policy submitted to the CBB, robust tools and documented experienced credit judgment, and the IFRS 9 three-stage approach.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module CM, Exposure Limit Rules consultation draft (XX 2025) with current table of contents
references.note: Shows Classification and Provisioning in CM-1.8 (last changed 04/2023) and the former sovereign provisioning section CM-1.10 deleted in 01/2023.

references.title: CBB Annual Report 2023
references.provision: Chapter 2, Amendments to the Credit Risk Management Module
references.note: January 2023 amendments: ECL on sovereign exposures under IFRS 9 per CM-1.8.

programs.title: Bahrain | Collateral Valuation and Management (Module CM)
programs.why: Where lending relies on collateral, Module CM requires independent third-party appraisals, regular revaluation and review by a qualified professional when values may have fallen. Credit administration staff must know these triggers and documentation standards.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module CM (Credit Risk Management), revised module consultation draft dated January 2019
references.note: Independent and timely third-party valuation where a loan depends on collateral; collateral cannot replace a full borrower assessment; property valued by a qualified professional when a material fall in value is indicated.

programs.title: Bahrain | Bahrain Credit Reference Bureau Reporting
programs.why: Banks feed and use the Bahrain Credit Reference Bureau (BCRB), and Module BC contains a section on credit check reports. The CBB has consulted on shorter retention of non-performing data (2020) and, in May 2026, on rules for updating BCRB records when cheques are returned. No training duty was found.

references.title: Proposal to Reduce the Retention Period of Non-Performing Facilities Data in the Credit Reference Bureau Report (EDBS/KH/C/15/2020)
references.note: Proposed keeping non-performing data for 3 years (retail) and 5 years (corporate) in BCRB reports.

references.title: Circular OG/166/2026: Consultation on Draft Resolutions under Law No. 23 of 2025 amending the Law of Commerce
references.note: Draft rules on partial cheque payment and on updating customer credit information at the BCRB for returned cheques; comments were due 1 June 2026.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module BC, November 2023 consultation copy with contents list
references.note: Contents list BC-4.12 Credit Check Reports among customer account rules.

programs.title: Bahrain | Consumer Finance Limits and Loan Insurance (Modules CM-5 and BC-4)
programs.why: Retail banks must keep total consumer debt repayments within a cap of gross income, assess each applicant's finances in detail, document exceptions for high earners and respect a maximum tenor. In November 2023 the CBB proposed cutting the cap from 50% to 40% and extending the tenor to ten years; the 2023 annual report says it was awaiting an industry proposal. Rules on insurance cover on loans add disclosure duties.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module CM Section CM-5.4, consultation mark-up (XX 2023)
references.note: Shows the total repayments ratio, affordability review, credit card treatment, high-earner exception and maximum tenor, with proposed changes marked.

references.title: Circular OG/401/2023: Consultation on Total Repayments Ratio and Maximum Tenor Limit
references.note: Proposed optional restructuring to a ten-year tenor without staging downgrade or rate increases; sent to retail banks and financing companies on 29 November 2023.

references.title: CBB Annual Report 2023
references.provision: Chapter 2, Consultation Paper: Total Repayments Ratio and Maximum Tenor Limit
references.note: States the proposed reduction to 40% and ten-year tenor and that the CBB was awaiting a proposal from the Bahrain Association of Banks.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module BC Section BC-4.21 Insurance Cover on Loans, consultation text (2023)
references.note: Proposed rules on recovering only the actual insurance cost, refunds, no commissions and full pre-contract disclosure of insurance terms.

programs.title: Bahrain | SME Financing Targets and Dedicated SME Units
programs.why: Following a 2021 consultation, the CBB told retail banks in October 2023 to scale SME lending towards 20% of the domestic financing portfolio by the end of 2025, set up a dedicated SME department or unit within credit and build SME-specific policies and products. Staff in those units need SME credit skills; no training is prescribed.

references.title: CBB Annual Report 2023
references.provision: Chapter 2, Financing to Small and Medium Sized Enterprises (SMEs) requirements
references.note: October 2023 circular: SME share targets of 5%, 10% and 20% by end-2023, 2024 and 2025, a dedicated SME unit and SME-specific policies and products.

references.title: Consultation EDBS/KH/C/9/2021: Proposed Requirements on Financing to SMEs
references.note: Original March 2021 proposal for phased SME targets and a dedicated SME unit with suitable resources.

programs.title: Bahrain | RTGS Participation and Payment System Oversight
programs.why: Banks settle through the CBB's RTGS system, whose operating guidelines require each member's payment gateway office to be staffed by qualified and authorised personnel, with tested back-up arrangements. The CBB's FMIs and Payment Oversight Framework (January 2024) sets the oversight approach to the systems banks participate in.

references.title: RTGS (Membership) Business Operating Guidelines, 2007
references.note: Members must keep secured gateways, tested disaster recovery and an office staffed by qualified, authorised personnel able to act for the member.

references.title: FMIs and Payment Oversight Framework (January 2024)
references.note: Sets out the CBB's objectives, standards and tools for overseeing payment systems and their participants, including banks.

programs.title: Bahrain | Cheques, E-Cheques and Returned Cheques
programs.why: Cheque handling is governed by Module BC (dishonoured cheques and post-dated cheques), the CBB's e-cheque service and, from Law No. 23 of 2025, new rules on partial payment of cheques and credit-bureau updates for returned cheques that the CBB consulted on in May 2026. No training duty was found; staff awareness is good practice.

references.title: Circular OG/166/2026: Consultation on Draft Resolutions under Law No. 23 of 2025 amending the Law of Commerce
references.note: Two draft resolutions for retail banks and BENEFIT: the Partial Cheque Payment System and BCRB updates for returned cheques.

references.title: CBB E-Cheque FAQs
references.note: Explains that e-cheques have the same legal force as paper cheques and how banks register and process them.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module BC, November 2023 consultation copy with contents list
references.provision: Table of contents, BC-5 and BC-5A
references.note: Contents list BC-5 Dishonoured Cheques and BC-5A Return Policy for post-dated cheques.

programs.title: Bahrain | Prudential Returns and CBB Reporting (Module BR, ICAAP and ST)
programs.why: Banks file prudential returns under Module BR and periodic submissions such as the annual ICAAP (by 31 May) and semi-annual stress test results; open banking statistics were added to BR in 2024. Reporting staff need to know the returns and deadlines; no training duty is prescribed.

references.title: Circular EDBS/KH/44/2018: Risk Management Related Modules (DS, RR, ICAAP and ST)
references.note: Sets annual ICAAP submission by 31 May from 2020, semi-annual stress test results (31 May and 30 November) and independent third-party reviews of the ICAAP and stress testing frameworks.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module BR, consultation extract (XX 2023)
references.note: Adds monthly reporting of open banking API availability and performance statistics by retail banks.

references.title: CBB Annual Report 2024
references.note: Reporting and disclosure requirements apply from the period ending 30 September 2024.

programs.title: Bahrain | FATCA Reporting under the Bahrain-US Agreement
programs.why: The CBB requires banks to report FATCA information each year through the national EOI portal under the Bahrain-US intergovernmental agreement and holds them responsible for accuracy. Staff doing due diligence and reporting need to know the rules; no training duty is set.

references.title: Directive OG/103/2026: AEOI - CRS and FATCA Reporting Window
references.note: Opens the reporting window for the 2025 year through the National Bureau for Revenue EOI portal and sets 2 May 2026 as the final date; FATCA reporting follows the Bahrain-US intergovernmental agreement and reporting institutions answer for accuracy and completeness.

programs.title: Bahrain | Common Reporting Standard Due Diligence and Reporting
programs.why: Bahrain uses the wider approach to the CRS and, under a January 2026 CBB directive, banks must apply the OECD's amended CRS, with reports filed yearly through the EOI portal. Accurate due diligence and reporting depend on knowledgeable staff; no training duty is set.

references.title: Directive OG/33/2026: Automatic Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes - Amended Common Reporting Standard
references.note: Requires banks and other reporting licensees to implement the OECD's 2023 amendments to the CRS and its Commentary, including the extended due diligence and reporting duties (e-money products, CBDCs, crypto-asset derivatives).

references.title: Directive OG/103/2026: AEOI - CRS and FATCA Reporting Window
references.note: Opens the reporting window for the 2025 year through the National Bureau for Revenue EOI portal and sets 2 May 2026 as the final date; FATCA reporting follows the Bahrain-US intergovernmental agreement and reporting institutions answer for accuracy and completeness.

programs.title: Bahrain | Audit Committee Oversight and External Audit Readiness (Module HC-3.4)
programs.why: Module HC requires audit committee members to have enough experience in audit, financial reporting and accounting, to meet the external auditor at least twice a year, review the integrity of financial statements and check the auditor's independence annually. This is a competence requirement for the committee and those who support it.

references.title: CBB Rulebook (Bank Licensees), High-Level Controls Module HC, consultation text of 18 July 2022
references.note: Audit committee members need sufficient audit, reporting and accounting experience; the committee meets the external auditor twice yearly, oversees financial reporting and audit scopes and assesses auditor independence each year.

programs.title: Bahrain | Open Banking Obligations for Retail Banks (Module GR-6)
programs.why: Retail banks must give licensed account information and payment initiation providers consent-based, non-discriminatory access to customer accounts through secure dedicated interfaces, with strong customer authentication. Since 1 September 2024 access covers legal persons and banks must support the embedded consent flow and report and disclose API performance. Staff building and supporting these channels need working knowledge of the rules.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module GR Chapter GR-6 Open Banking, consultation text (XX 2023)
references.note: Access for AISPs and PISPs on customer consent and PDPL terms, dedicated interface standards, security of sessions and credentials, and contingency measures.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module PD, consultation extract (XX 2023)
references.note: Retail banks disclose open banking API performance statistics on their websites each quarter.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 5, Module OB (Open Banking), consultation extract (XX 2023)
references.note: Scope of the providers that access accounts held by conventional retail banks.

references.title: CBB Annual Report 2024
references.note: May 2024 final amendments: legal persons included, embedded flow required, new requirements effective 1 September 2024.

programs.title: Bahrain | Digital Onboarding and the National E-KYC System (Module FC-1)
programs.why: Module FC limits digital onboarding of customers living outside the GCC and ties remote identification to the National E-KYC system, alongside the CDD and non-resident rules. Onboarding staff must apply these limits correctly; this is a competence duty under the CDD rules rather than a set course.

references.title: CBB Rulebook Volume 1, Module FC, 2023 consultation copy
references.note: Digital onboarding is not allowed for natural persons living outside the GCC except named categories, with the National E-KYC system used for identification and non-resident CDD rules applied.

programs.title: Bahrain | CBB Regulatory Sandbox and Fintech Partnerships
programs.why: The CBB's Regulatory Sandbox Framework (revised December 2021) is open to licensed banks and fintechs. Participants must show innovation and customer benefit, identify major risks including continuity, meet CDD and AML/CFT rules and protect customer confidentiality during a test of up to 12 months, then exit in an orderly way. Teams running a test need to understand these conditions.

references.title: CBB FinTech and Innovation page: Regulatory Sandbox Framework
references.note: Sets eligibility (innovation, customer benefit, risk identification, CDD/AML compliance, confidentiality), a testing period of up to 12 months with extensions, and exit conditions.

references.title: CBB Application for Regulatory Sandbox (2021)
references.note: Application asks for test plans, timeframes, volunteer customers, thresholds and safeguards for customer information.

references.title: Central Bank of Bahrain Enhances Fintech Regulatory Sandbox to Boost Innovation (7 December 2021)
references.note: Announces the revised framework with stricter eligibility and a streamlined process, open to licensees and other firms.

notes: Module FP (Fit and Proper Requirements) was issued in March 2025 in the Common Volume of the Rulebook and replaced the fit and proper parts of the LR, AU and TC modules; prior-approval rules applied from 1 April 2025 and the rest from 1 October 2025.

A revised High-Level Controls Module for bank licensees, consulted on in July 2022, was issued in March 2023 and its new rules took effect on 1 October 2023 (CBB Annual Report 2023); director training sits in HC-2.3 and compliance, risk and audit staff training in HC-7 to HC-9. Provisions are read from the CBB-hosted consultation text. An earlier note dating application from April 2023 was wrong.

Module FC was amended after consultations in 2023 (second consultation feedback December 2023), notably on companies under formation and non-resident customers; the CBB website also carries an updated public version of the national risk assessment report (Arabic, uploaded August 2026).

Decree-Law 4 of 2001 has been amended several times (including 2006, 2013, 2017 and 2020). Press and secondary sources report a further Decree-Law No. 36 of 2025 widening the offences and giving the financial intelligence centre power to suspend transactions for up to 72 hours; this was not confirmed on an official site from this session.

Cyber: the CBB consulted in January 2024 on further amendments to the cyber security rules in Module OM-5.5, and in November 2022 on the NCSC's draft Financial Cybersecurity Controls for all licensees. Whether that national standard has been finalised was not confirmed.
Tax reporting: Directive OG/33/2026 (January 2026) requires implementation of the OECD's amended Common Reporting Standard; CRS and FATCA reports for 2025 were due by 2 May 2026 via the EOI portal.

Access limits: the consolidated Rulebook (cbben.thomsonreuters.com) returned 403, and lloc.gov.bh, pdp.gov.bh, interior.gov.bh and other government hosts were not reachable from this session. Rulebook provisions cited without a check date need confirming against the in-force text.

A CBB-hosted 2021 consultation copy of Module FC (cbb.gov.bh/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/Consultation_Vol-1_FC_E-KYC.pdf) contains an FC-6 staff training chapter (new staff trained within three months; training normally once a year), but the 2023 contents list shows FC-6.1 last changed in 01/2022, so the current wording is unconfirmed and AML training stays at competence until the current FC-6 text is checked.

Prudential pipeline: the draft IRRBB module (January 2024) and the second consultation on Module CA credit risk (July 2024) were still under study per the CBB Annual Report 2024; new exposure limit rules for CM-2 were consulted on in March 2025 and revised initial capital in February 2026. In April 2026 the CBB launched a loan deferral and liquidity support programme, cutting minimum LCR and NSFR from 100% to 80% and the reserve requirement from 5% to 3.5%.

Lending and payments: in November 2023 the CBB proposed cutting the consumer debt-service cap from 50% to 40% with ten-year tenors (outcome not confirmed officially); retail banks had a 20% SME lending target for end-2025; open banking covers legal persons from 1 September 2024; in May 2026 the CBB consulted on partial cheque payments and credit-bureau updates for returned cheques under Law No. 23 of 2025. A February 2026 payment services module covers PSPs, not banks.
